objectives: Choose an algorithm from the constraints before writing code.

params.title: Problem B

screens.question: Which solution passes every test inside 1 second?

options.why: You read three loops as fine. At $n = 2 \cdot 10^5$ the slices add up to about $10^{15}$ steps.

options.text:
```python
best = a[0]
for l in range(n):
    s = 0
    for r in range(l, n):
        s += a[r]
        best = max(best, s)
```
options.why: Two loops over $2 \cdot 10^5$ days is about $2 \cdot 10^{10}$ steps: minutes, not a second.

options.text:
```python
best = cur = a[0]
for x in a[1:]:
    cur = max(x, cur + x)
    best = max(best, cur)
```

screens.title: Constraints to complexity
screens.prose: What you just did has a name: turning a **constraint** into an **allowed complexity**. Use about $10^8$ steps for a 1 s limit. Python manages far fewer, so on Codeforces submit it as **PyPy 3**, or write C++.

hints.text: Put each largest $n$ into each growth and compare with $10^8$.
The rows read $2^n$, $n^3$, $n^2$ and $n \log n$. A value of $10^{18}$ allows only $\log n$.

feedback.correct: Each row is the slowest growth that still lands near $10^8$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put the largest $n$ into your growth and compare with $10^8$.

byKey.r0c1: Your entry for $n \le 20$ is not the slowest that fits. $2^{20} \approx 10^6$, so trying every subset fits.
byKey.r1c1: Your entry for $n \le 500$ is not the slowest that fits. $500^3 = 1.25 \cdot 10^8$ fits, just.
byKey.r2c1: Your entry for $n \le 5{,}000$ is not the slowest that fits. $5{,}000^2 = 2.5 \cdot 10^7$ fits.
byKey.r4c1: Your entry for $10^{18}$ is too slow. You cannot even count to $10^{18}$ in time; only halving fits.

explain.text: You read each limit as the setter's hint about the intended solution. Small limits allow brute force; large ones demand $n \log n$ or better. A limit on a value rather than a length, like $10^{18}$, asks for $\log$.

params.title: Problem D

screens.question: How many sets must a program try to check every one at $n = 20$?

hints.text: Each instrument is either in the set or out.
The constraint caps $n$ at 20.
Two choices, 20 times: $2^{20}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each instrument is in or out, independently.

byKey.n2: That is $n^2$. Each instrument doubles the count, so it is $2^{20}$.
byKey.n: That counts the instruments. Every in-or-out pattern is a different set.
byKey.n3: That is $n^3$. Each instrument doubles the count, so it is $2^{20}$.

explain.text: You counted $2^{20} \approx 10^6$ sets. Adding up each set's risk costs up to 20 more steps: about $2 \cdot 10^7$ in all, fine in C++. A limit of 20 says try everything, which level 3 does with bitmasks.

params.title: Problem E

screens.question: How many pairs $i < j$ are there when $n = 5{,}000$?

hints.text: Each pair is counted once, with $i < j$.
The number of pairs is $n(n-1)/2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count each unordered pair once.

byKey.ordered: That is $n^2$, which counts $(i, j)$ and $(j, i)$ and $(i, i)$. Halve it and drop the diagonal.
byKey.ordered2: That counts each pair twice, once each way round. Halve it.

explain.text: About $1.25 \cdot 10^7$ pairs is a tenth of a second in C++. In plain Python it takes a few seconds, so submit it as PyPy 3 or in C++. A limit of 5,000 says $O(n^2)$ is intended.

params.title: Problem F

screens.question: Binary search for $m$ between 0 and $10^9$. How many halvings shrink those $10^9 + 1$ values to one?

hints.text: Each halving cuts the range in two.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count how often you can halve $10^9$ before one value is left.

byKey.linear: That tries every $m$ in turn. Halving reaches one value far sooner.
byKey.sqrt: That is $\sqrt{10^9}$. Halving needs only the logarithm, $\log_2 10^9 \approx 30$.

explain.text: You need about 30 halvings, so $2 \cdot 10^5$ queries cost about $6 \cdot 10^6$ steps. A value of $10^{18}$ can be halved but never scanned. Huge values with many queries ask for $O(\log)$ per query.

params.title: Problem G, input

screens.question: What is the most total work any input can force?

options.why: You chose a gentle split. The setter picks the worst one, and one large test is worst for $n^2$.
You ignored the sum bound. All the tests together hold at most $2 \cdot 10^5$ values.

hints.text: The tests must share $2 \cdot 10^5$ values. Which split makes $\sum n_i^2$ largest?
Squares reward putting everything in one test.

feedback.correct: One big test case gives $(2 \cdot 10^5)^2 = 4 \cdot 10^{10}$: too slow.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the split of $2 \cdot 10^5$ values that makes $\sum n_i^2$ largest.

byKey.even: You split the values evenly. The setter will also send one test with all $2 \cdot 10^5$ values.

explain.text: The sum bound makes linear work safe across tests, but not quadratic work. $\sum n_i^2$ is largest when one test holds everything: $4 \cdot 10^{10}$. So per-test complexity is judged at the full $2 \cdot 10^5$.

screens.title: One loop, how many steps?
screens.prose: This solution counts the distinct P&L values for $n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$. It has one loop.
screens.question: About how many steps can it take at $n = 2 \cdot 10^5$?

options.why: You counted the loop. `x not in seen` reads `seen` from the start each time: up to $n$ steps inside.
That would need a sorted list and binary search. `in` on a list reads it item by item.

hints.text: What does `x not in seen` do on a list?
Line 3 compares `x` with every item of `seen`.
With all values distinct, `seen` grows to $n$, so the checks add up to about $n^2/2 = 2 \cdot 10^{10}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the work inside line 3, not only the loop.

byKey.loop: You counted the loop but not line 3. `in` on a list scans it: about $2 \cdot 10^{10}$ steps in all.

explain.text: Line 3 scans up to $n$ items, so the loop costs about $2 \cdot 10^{10}$ steps. A `set` makes the check $O(1)$ on average (`ds`, Looking up in constant time). `list.pop(0)` and `s = s + c` hide costs like this too.

screens.title: The budget rule
screens.prose:
Each time, you compared the step count at the largest input with the budget.

$$\text{steps}(n_{\max}) \le 10^8 \times \text{seconds}$$

Python's budget is a few to a hundred times smaller.

params.title: budget_class

screens.question: Write `budget_class(n)`.

widget.starter:
from math import log2

# from the most work to the least
CLASSES = ["2^n", "n^3", "n^2", "n log n", "n", "log n"]


def budget_class(n):
    ...
widget.how: Check runs 15 hidden tests, from $n = 1$ to $n = 10^{18}$, including each side of every boundary. Answers are compared exactly as strings.

hints.text: Try the classes in order and return the first that fits.
Python computes `2 ** n` exactly, so at $n = 10^{18}$ it never finishes. Check $n$ first.
`if n <= 60 and 2 ** n <= 10 ** 8:` then the same test for `n ** 3`, `n ** 2`, `n * log2(n)` and `n`; else `"log n"`.

feedback.correct: Six checks in order, with a guard before `2 ** n`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first failing test.

byKey.test-7: Test 7 has $n = 500$: $500^3 = 1.25 \cdot 10^8$ is just over, so the answer is `"n^2"`. The table's 500 is a rule of thumb.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 has $n = 465$: $465^3 \approx 1.005 \cdot 10^8$, just over the budget.
byKey.test-15: Test 15 has $n = 10^{18}$. Computing `2 ** n` there never ends; check $n$ before the power.

explain.text: The boundaries sit at $n = 26$, 464, $10^4$, about $4.5 \cdot 10^6$ and $10^8$. At $n = 500$ the exact rule says $n^2$ while the table says $n^3$: the table rounds to about a second. The guard `n <= 60` stops Python building a number with $10^{18}$ bits.

Count pairs i < j with aᵢ + aⱼ ≤ k.
params.title: Problem H

screens.question: Write `pair_sums_at_most(xs, k)`.

tests.setup: import random; r = random.Random(11); ys = [r.randint(-1000, 1000) for _ in range(1000)]
import random; r = random.Random(5); xs = [r.randint(-10**9, 10**9) for _ in range(200000)]

widget.how: Check runs 9 hidden tests: hand cases with duplicates, negative values and $n = 1$. Test 8 passes 1,000 values in a list that counts how often it is read; at most 20,000 reads pass. Test 9 has 200,000 values, so an $O(n^2)$ loop is stopped.

hints.text: After sorting, if the smallest and largest values fit, so does the smallest with everything below the largest.
Keep `i` at the small end and `j` at the large end of the sorted list.
If `a[i] + a[j] <= k`, add `j - i` and move `i` up; otherwise move `j` down. Stop when they meet.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first failing test.

byKey.test-3: Test 3 is four 2s with $k = 4$ and expects 6. Equal values still make pairs: use `<=`.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 has negative values and a negative $k$. Do not start any count or bound at 0.
byKey.test-8: Test 8 counted far more than 20,000 reads of the list. Checking every pair reads it about $n^2$ times.
byKey.test-9: Test 9 has 200,000 values. Checking every pair is $2 \cdot 10^{10}$ steps; sort and use two pointers.

explain.text: Sorting costs $O(n \log n)$ and the two pointers then meet in at most $n$ moves. When `a[i] + a[j] <= k`, every partner between `i` and `j` also fits, so one step counts `j - i` pairs. In Pyodide the 200,000-value test takes well under a second.

screens.title: What are the constraints?
screens.prose: In a developer interview at a trading firm, the first good question is the one from this lesson. Then say the complexity out loud before you code: interviewers mark that habit.

lines: Interviewer: Here are a day's trade prices.
Find two trades whose prices sum
below £10⁶. A second or two is fine.
params.title: Interview

screens.question: Which plan do you state first?

options.text: Sort, then two pointers from both ends: $O(n \log n)$, about $2 \cdot 10^7$ steps
Check every pair: $O(n^2)$, simple and safe
options.why: You skipped the constraint. $10^6$ trades make about $5 \cdot 10^{11}$ pairs.
A hash set finds an exact sum. *Closest* needs order, which sorting gives.

hints.text: Compute the pair count at $n = 10^6$.
Sorting costs $10^6 \log_2 10^6 \approx 2 \cdot 10^7$ steps; the two pointers add $10^6$.

feedback.correct: Constraints, then complexity, then code: the order interviewers want to hear.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $n = 10^6$ into each plan's step count.

byKey.pairs: You chose every pair. At $10^6$ trades that is $5 \cdot 10^{11}$ checks, hours of work.

explain.text: Asking for the constraints turned a vague task into a budget: $n = 10^6$ allows $O(n \log n)$ but not $O(n^2)$. Saying "sort, then two pointers, $O(n \log n)$" before coding shows the interviewer the plan fits.

ideas: Before coding, count steps at the largest input: about $10^8$ a second in C++, far fewer in Python.
Small limits invite brute force: $2^n$ for $n \le 20$, $n^2$ for $n \le 5{,}000$. Larger ones ask for $n \log n$, and a value of $10^{18}$ for $\log$.
Count the hidden cost inside a loop: `in` on a list, `pop(0)` and string `+` are each $O(n)$.

formula.name: The budget rule
formula.note: For C++; use PyPy 3 or C++ when Python's budget is too small.

summary.trap: One loop is not one step per item: `x in some_list` scans the list, so the loop is $O(n^2)$.

quiz.prose: A statement has $n \le 100$ and a 1 s limit. You see a clever $O(n \log n)$ idea needing 20 minutes of careful code. An $O(n^3)$ triple loop takes 3.
quiz.question: Which do you write?

options.text: The clever idea: it is the faster algorithm
options.why: You chose speed you do not need. $100^3 = 10^6$ steps already fit many times over.
You judged the growth, not the count. At $n = 100$ it is only $10^6$ steps.

explain.text: The constraint says brute force is enough, so the simple code is the right code. It is also less likely to hold a bug, and it saves 17 minutes.

quiz.prose:
A breadth-first search over $2 \cdot 10^5$ nodes keeps its queue in a Python list:

```python
while queue:
    node = queue.pop(0)
    ...
```
quiz.question: What does `queue.pop(0)` cost over the whole search?

options.text: Up to about $n^2/2 = 2 \cdot 10^{10}$ moves: each pop shifts the list

options.why: You counted the pops. Each `pop(0)` shifts every remaining item one place left.
A list is not a heap. Removing its first item moves all the others.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what happens to the other items when the first one goes.

explain.text: Removing the first item of a list shifts the rest, so a long queue costs $O(n)$ per pop. `collections.deque` pops from the front in $O(1)$ (`ds`, First in, first out).

quiz.prose: $n \le 10^6$. Your plan sorts the values once.
quiz.question: About how many steps is that?

options.why: That leaves out the $\log_2 n \approx 20$ factor of sorting.
That is $n^2$. A good sort is $n \log n$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Sorting costs $n \log_2 n$.

explain.text: $\log_2 10^6 \approx 19.9$, so the sort is about $2 \cdot 10^7$ steps: a fifth of a second in C++.

quiz.prose: A statement allows $n \le 400$ with a 2 s limit.
quiz.question: Which complexity is the setter most likely inviting?

options.why: $2^{400}$ is astronomically large. Trying every subset needs $n$ near 20.
That would pass, but a limit as small as 400 would then be odd. Setters size the limit to the intended solution.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put 400 into each growth.

explain.text: $400^3 = 6.4 \cdot 10^7$ fits in 2 s with room to spare. Setters choose limits that let the intended solution pass and the next slower one fail.
